CausalChain: NAFLD → increased de novo lipogenesis → elevated cholesterol synthesis and conjugated bile acids → activation of FXR signaling in hepatocytes → reprogramming of sphingolipid metabolism (upregulation of sphingosine kinase) → increased S1P production → activation of oncogenic pathways (e.g., YAP/AKT) and suppression of p53-mediated apoptosis, as well as modulation of the tumor immune microenvironment → promotion of HCC progression.
Hypothesis: Elevated conjugated bile acids in NAFLD activate FXR in hepatocytes, which reprograms sphingolipid metabolism to increase S1P production; this surge in S1P fosters an immunosuppressive, pro-oncogenic microenvironment that facilitates the transition from fatty liver to hepatocellular carcinoma. Targeting the FXR–sphingolipid axis may represent a novel therapeutic strategy for NAFLD-associated HCC.
Abstract: In the context of non‐alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) and its progression to hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), emerging evidence suggests that multiple lipid metabolic pathways are rewired. In particular, increased de novo lipogenesis leads to higher levels of cholesterol and conjugated bile acids, which in turn activate nuclear receptors such as FXR. FXR activation appears to influence sphingolipid metabolism, including the upregulation of sphingosine kinase and subsequent elevation of sphingosine‐1‐phosphate (S1P), a lipid mediator known to promote oncogenic signaling and mediate immune evasion. These converging metabolic alterations may create a microenvironment that favors tumor growth and resistance to apoptosis while impairing innate immune surveillance. This hypothesis posits that an FXR‐dependent conversion of bile acids into pro‐oncogenic sphingolipid signals serves as a missing link between fatty liver disease and liver cancer progression. Targeting this axis could offer novel therapeutic opportunities in NAFLD‐associated HCC.
